title: Troubleshooting: Scissors Won’t Cut Through Thick Rosemary Stems
meta_description: Struggling with woody herbs? Learn how to handle herb scissors thick rosemary troubleshooting and keep your multi-blade shears cutting sharp.
html:
There is nothing more frustrating than being in the middle of prepping a roast or a focaccia, only to have your shears stop halfway through a sprig of rosemary. You squeeze, the blades bend slightly, and the woody stem just refuses to give way. If you're dealing with herb scissors thick rosemary troubleshooting, you aren't alone; rosemary is essentially a miniature pine tree, and its lignified stems are a different beast compared to soft basil or cilantro.

Why Rosemary Stems Defeat Most Herb Scissors

Most multi-blade shears are designed for "soft herbs." This means they are engineered to slice through thin, water-rich stems and delicate leaves. Rosemary, however, develops a woody core as it ages. When you try to push five blades through a thick, fibrous stem simultaneously, the resistance is five times higher than it would be with a single pair of scissors.

If the blades aren't perfectly aligned or if the tension in the pivot screw is too loose, the blades will slide past each other instead of shearing. This results in the stem getting crushed or jammed between the blades rather than being cut clean.

Immediate Fixes for Herb Scissors Thick Rosemary Troubleshooting

Before you toss your shears into the junk drawer, try these practical adjustments to get through those stubborn stems:

  • Check the Pivot Tension: If the handles feel "wobbly," the blades aren't meeting with enough pressure. If your model allows, slightly tighten the center screw.
  • The Angle of Attack: Don't cut perpendicular to the stem. Try cutting at a 45-degree angle. This reduces the surface area the blades have to penetrate at once, making it easier to break through the woody exterior.
  • Avoid the Base: The thickest part of the rosemary plant is at the bottom of the stem. Use your shears for the leafy tops and switch to a heavy-duty kitchen knife for the woody base.
  • Clean the Gaps: Dried herb resin can build up between multi-blades, creating a microscopic gap that prevents a clean snip. Use a cleaning comb to clear out debris.

The Right Tool for the Right Herb

It is important to recognize that not all shears are created equal. If you are using a high-efficiency tool like the Herb Scissors—the five-blade herb shears that mince cilantro, chives, and basil in one snip—you are using a tool optimized for speed and volume of soft greens. These are absolute game-changers for making chimichurri or chopping parsley for a garnish.

However, the secret to longevity for these tools is knowing when not to use them. Forcing five blades through a pencil-thick rosemary stem can put undue stress on the pivot point and potentially dull the edges of the blades. To keep your Herb Scissors in peak condition, stick to the "soft and leafy" rule. For the woody stems, a single-blade heavy-duty kitchen shear or a chef's knife is the safer bet.

Maintaining Your Blades for Maximum Efficiency

When you encounter herb scissors thick rosemary troubleshooting, it's often a sign that your blades have lost their "bite." Even if you aren't cutting thick stems, a buildup of oils and minerals from your water can dull the stainless steel over time.

To keep your shears sharp, always hand-wash them immediately after use. Dishwashers can cause micro-corrosion on the blade edges. If you've been using your Herb Scissors for a while and notice they are sliding rather than slicing, use the included cleaning comb to remove any trapped fibers from the inner pivot. This ensures the blades close completely, which is essential for cutting through the tougher side of the herb spectrum.

How to Prep Rosemary for Multi-Blade Shears

If you really want the speed of multi-blade shearing for rosemary, you just need to prep the herb first. Instead of trying to chop the entire sprig, strip the needles off the woody stem by hand. Run your fingers down the stem in the opposite direction of growth, and the leaves will pop right off.

Once you have a pile of loose rosemary needles, you can use your Herb Scissors to mince them into fine pieces in seconds. This protects your equipment and gives you a much more consistent chop for your recipes, avoiding those chunky, woody bits that can ruin a delicate sauce.

FAQ

Can I sharpen my multi-blade herb scissors?

It is difficult to sharpen multi-blade shears at home because of the tight spacing between the blades. Your best bet is to prevent dulling by avoiding woody stems and keeping them clean with a cleaning comb.

Why do my scissors chew the herb instead of cutting it?

This usually happens when the blades are dull or the pivot is too loose. The blades "fold" the herb instead of slicing it. Check your tension and ensure there is no debris trapped in the hinge.

Are five-blade scissors better than single-blade scissors?

For volume and speed, yes. Tools like the Herb Scissors allow you to mince large amounts of soft herbs in a fraction of the time. For heavy-duty pruning or cutting thick stems, a single-blade shear is more powerful.
